beats.goal: Address the viewer directly, name the skill of spotting misleading charts, and show why it matters in daily life.
beats.example_or_visual: Say: 'You've probably scrolled past a chart today that was quietly lying to you.' Show a news-style bar chart titled 'Crime Is Skyrocketing!' where one bar looks about five times taller than the other, then ask, 'But what if I told you the two numbers are 52 and 50?'

beats.goal: Anchor in something the viewer already knows (bar charts), then work the truncated-axis trick with named variables.
beats.example_or_visual: Redraw the chart live with two bars, A = 52 burglaries per 1,000 and B = 50 per 1,000. First, the y-axis starts at 49, so A looks 3x as tall as B. Narrate: 'let me pick a red-- no, a green marker for the axis.' Redraw with the axis starting at 0, and the bars look nearly identical. Compute the real difference: (52 − 50)/50 = 4%.

beats.goal: Narrate a live side-by-side drawing so the viewer sees how the axis start alone changes the story.
beats.example_or_visual: Draw two panels side by side with the same data. Left: axis 49–53, bars labeled A and B with a dramatic gap. Right: axis 0–60, bars almost level. Circle the axis baseline in a different color: 'I'd take this orange-- let me use blue so it stands out.' Label the panels 'Zoomed' and 'Honest'.

beats.goal: State the general rule in full sentences: a chart's visual size should be proportional to the quantity it represents.
beats.example_or_visual: Say: 'We would define a misleading chart as one where the visual change is bigger or smaller than the real change in the numbers.' Introduce the 'lie factor' (Edward Tufte's term): size of effect shown in the graphic divided by size of effect in the data. For the chart above, lie factor = 200% ÷ 4% = 50.

beats.goal: Use a rhetorical question to pivot from bar charts to a trickier case, where the numbers themselves are fine but the framing is not.
beats.example_or_visual: Ask: 'But what if the axis is perfectly honest and the chart still misleads you?' Preview a line chart of a town's monthly unemployment rate, 5.1% to 4.9% over 3 months, then the same data shown over 10 years.

beats.goal: Show cherry-picking of time windows with a worked example the viewer can verify, with a callback to the axis trick.
beats.example_or_visual: A company ad says 'Our stock is up 30%!' using a window from March 1 ($100) to June 1 ($130). Draw the full-year line: the stock was $200 in January and fell to $100 by March. Draw the window as a small green box on the full curve. Compute the full-year change: (130 − 200)/200 = −35%. Callback: 'Remember the zoomed panel? Same trick, different axis: time.'

beats.goal: Close with a checklist of questions to ask of any chart and preview the next video on misleading averages, ending with encouragement.
beats.example_or_visual: Write three questions on the board: 'Where does the axis start? What window of time? Compared to what?' Then say: 'Next time, we'll look at how the word "average" can mean mean, median, or mode, and why a company with a $50,000 "average" salary might pay most people $30,000.' End: 'You've already got the first three tools, so you'll be ready.'
